::: {#def-valid-p-value}
#### Valid p-value

A [p-value](inference.qmd#def-p-value) $p$ for a null hypothesis $H_0$ is **valid** if,
when $H_0$ is true, it is stochastically no smaller than a uniform random variable:

$$\Pr_{H_0}(p \le u) \le u \quad \text{for every } u \in [0, 1].$$

If the inequality is an equality, $p$ is uniform on $[0, 1]$ under $H_0$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-valid-p-value}
#### The two-sided z-test p-value is valid

For a standard Gaussian statistic $Z$, the p-value $p = 2 \normcdf(-\abs{Z})$
is the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is at least as extreme as $Z$.
Because $Z$ has a continuous distribution, this p-value is uniform on $[0, 1]$,
so $\Pr(p \le u) = u$ exactly.
Simulating $10^5$ true null hypotheses checks this:

```{r}
#| label: valid-p-value
#| code-fold: false
set.seed(573)
p_null <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(1e5)))
u <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5)
data.frame(u = u, fraction_at_most_u = sapply(u, function(x) mean(p_null <= x)))
```

Each fraction is close to its $u$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-valid-p-value-discrete}
#### Discrete statistics give conservative p-values

When the test statistic is discrete, as in
[Fisher's exact test](categorical-tests.qmd#def-fishers-exact),
a p-value can satisfy $\Pr_{H_0}(p \le u) < u$ for some $u$.
It is still valid, but conservative:
it rejects a true null hypothesis less often than its nominal level.
:::
